name: Psoriasis
description: Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune condition where skin cells multiply much faster than normal. This causes thick, red, raised patches covered with silvery-white scales, commonly on the elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back.
common_symptoms: Raised, inflamed, red patches of skin (may appear purplish or dark brown on darker skin)
Thick silvery-white or grayish scales on top of the patches
Dry, cracked skin that may bleed when stretched
Itching, burning, or soreness around the patches
Pitted, ridged, or thickened fingernails or toenails
Stiff, swollen, or painful joints (in psoriatic arthritis)
causes: An autoimmune reaction where T-cells mistakenly attack healthy skin cells
Excessively rapid skin cell turnover (taking days instead of weeks to shed)
risk_factors: Family history of psoriasis or autoimmune diseases
Skin injuries (cuts, scrapes, sunburns, bug bites - Koebner phenomenon)
Infections such as strep throat, cold dry weather, smoking, and heavy alcohol use
first_aid: Apply soothing emollients or moisturizing ointment to soften scales
Take a short lukewarm bath with colloidal oatmeal or bath oils to ease discomfort
Do not pull, peel, or forcibly pick off silvery scales
precautions: Avoid cold, dry weather exposure without protective warm clothing
Use a humidifier indoors during winter months
Wear loose, soft clothing that minimizes friction against skin plaques
home_care: Keep skin well moisturized with thick creams or ointments
Take daily baths with gentle cleansers to soften and wash away loose scales
Get moderate, safe sunlight exposure (consult your doctor for recommended minutes)
do_not: DO NOT aggressively peel or scrape off scales, as this can trigger worse patches (Koebner reaction)
DO NOT bathe in very hot water or scrub with harsh loofahs
DO NOT stop prescribed treatments abruptly without consulting your doctor
red_flags: Plaques suddenly cover more than 80-90% of the body with redness and peeling (erythrodermic psoriasis - emergency)
Widespread small blisters filled with pus accompanied by fever and chills (generalized pustular psoriasis)
Severe joint pain, warmth, and swelling in fingers, knees, or spine
when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor or dermatologist if you suspect you have psoriasis, if patches cause severe discomfort, or if you develop joint stiffness and pain.
prevention: Keep skin moisturized to prevent cracking
Avoid skin trauma, scratches, and sunburns
Quit smoking and limit alcohol consumption
Practice stress-relief techniques like meditation and regular exercise
